bib.title: RACE: Large-scale ReAding Comprehension Dataset From Examinations

question: Can a large multiple-choice reading comprehension dataset written by human experts for school exams be built that needs more reasoning than existing datasets and separates machines from humans?
hypothesis: Existing datasets (cloze, span-based) are solvable by matching and are noisy; an exam-derived dataset with free-form options will be harder and show a large machine-human gap.
contributions: RACE: 27,933 passages and 97,687 expert-written four-option questions from Chinese middle and high school English exams
Annotation of reasoning types showing 59.2% of questions need single- or multi-sentence reasoning
Baselines (sliding window, Stanford AR, Gated-Attention Reader) vs. Turker and ceiling human performance

method.summary: Raw exam reading problems were scraped from three Chinese public websites and filtered to 27,933 passages and 97,687 four-option questions. Question reasoning types were labelled by Mechanical Turk on 500 questions. Three baselines were trained on RACE-M plus RACE-H and compared with Turkers and a human ceiling.

datasets.name: RACE (RACE-M + RACE-H)
datasets.split: Train 25,137 passages / 87,866 questions; Dev 1,389 / 4,887; Test 1,407 / 4,934 (5% dev, 5% test for each of RACE-M and RACE-H)
datasets.source: English exams by teachers in China, scraped from 21cnjy.com, 5utk.ks5u.com, zujuan.xkw.com; raw 137,918 passages and 519,878 questions (middle 38,159 / 156,782; high 99,759 / 363,096)
datasets.preprocessing: removed questions not having four options; removed items with images or tables; removed questions with keywords 'underlined' or 'paragraph'; removed duplicate articles; for xkw.com answers stored as images, OCR with tesseract and ABBYY FineReader, dropped answers where the two disagreed

datasets.name: Reasoning-type annotation sample
datasets.split: sample (the paper later calls it a randomly sampled subset of the test set)
datasets.source: Amazon Mechanical Turk, master turkers only, two labels per question, $0.70 per RACE-M passage and $1.00 per RACE-H passage

models.name: Sliding Window
models.architecture: rule-based TF-IDF-style matching of question+answer against text windows (Richardson et al. 2013)

other.window size: chosen by performance on train and dev sets; value not stated

models.name: Stanford Attentive Reader
models.architecture: bidirectional GRU encoders for passage, question and options, bilinear attention

models.name: Gated-Attention Reader (GA)
models.architecture: multi-hop gated attention reader; Attention Sum layer not applied at final layer; no character-level embeddings

training.objective: inferred: cross-entropy over softmax of four option scores (Eq. 2); loss not named
training.regularisation: gradient clipped when norm larger than 10

other.init: GRU weights N(0, 0.1); other parameters uniform (-0.01, 0.01)
other.data: RACE-M and RACE-H used together to train, tested separately

inference.decoding: argmax over softmax of option scores

metrics.name: ceiling human performance
metrics.definition: share of questions that are valid (unambiguous and having a correct answer), labelled manually

eval.protocol: Single run per model; no seeds or significance test stated. Turker accuracy on 500 sampled questions. Comparison datasets (MCTest, CNN/DM, CBT, WDW) numbers taken from prior publications.

evidence.quote: learning rate to 0.1 for Stanford AR and 0.3 for GA and dropout rate to 0.5

results.setup: Full RACE after filtering of 519,878 raw questions
results.quote: Finally, we get the cleaned dataset RACE, with 27,933 passages and 97,687 questions.

results.claim: Stanford Attentive Reader reaches 43.3% accuracy on RACE.
results.setup: Trained on RACE-M+RACE-H train, tested on RACE test, GloVe-100, hidden 128, 1 layer, SGD lr 0.1
results.quote: The Stanford AR and Gated AR achieve an accuracy of only 43.3% and 44.1% on RACE
results.table: Table 5, row Stanford AR, column RACE

results.claim: Gated-Attention Reader reaches 44.1% accuracy on RACE, the best model result.
results.quote: The Stanford AR and Gated AR achieve an accuracy of only 43.3% and 44.1% on RACE
results.note: Abstract rounds state of the art to 43%

results.claim: Ceiling human performance on RACE is 94.5% (share of valid questions).
results.setup: Authors manually labelled the proportion of valid (unambiguous, correct-answer) questions; sample size for this check not stated
results.quote: We found that 94.5% of the data is valid, which sets the ceiling human performance.

results.claim: Mechanical Turkers score 73.3% on RACE overall (85.1 RACE-M, 69.4 RACE-H).
results.setup: 500 sampled questions, half RACE-M and half RACE-H, master turkers
results.quote: The turkers’ performance is 85% for RACE-M and 70% for RACE-H.
results.note: Text rounds to 85% and 70%; Table 5 prints 85.1, 69.4, 73.3

results.claim: 59.2% of RACE questions need single- or multi-sentence reasoning, vs 21% CNN, 20.5% SQuAD, 33.9% NewsQA.
results.setup: 500 questions labelled by two Turkers each; CNN, SQuAD, NewsQA figures from Chen et al. 2016 and Trischler et al. 2016
results.quote: Specifically, 59.2% questions of RACE are either in the category of single-sentence reasoning or in the category of multi-sentence reasoning

results.claim: Only 15.8% of RACE questions are word-matching, the lowest among categories.
results.quote: Also notice that the ratio of word matching questions on RACE is only 15.8%
results.table: Table 4, row Word Matching, column RACE

results.claim: Sliding window scores 37.3% on RACE-M and 30.4% on RACE-H, 32.2% on RACE, versus 51.5% on MCTest.
results.setup: Rule-based baseline; MCTest 51.5 quoted from Richardson et al. 2013
results.quote: Sliding Window achieves an accuracy of 51.5% on MCTest while only 37.3% on RACE
results.table: Table 5, row Sliding Window, column RACE
results.note: Text says 37.3% on RACE but that is the RACE-M cell; RACE overall is 32.2

results.claim: Sliding window beats random by 28.6% on RACE vs 58.5%, 92.2%, 50% on CBT-N, CBT-C, WDW, so RACE is less solvable by matching.
results.quote: On RACE, Sliding Window is 28.6% better than the random baseline
results.note: Ten options on CBT, about three on WDW, so not directly comparable

results.claim: Gap between best model and Turkers is 41% on RACE-M and 25% on RACE-H.
results.quote: The performance gap is 41% for the middle school problems and 25% for the high school problems.

limits: Vocabulary and language constructs are simpler than news or Wikipedia because passages target foreign-language learners (Sec 3.1).
Turker accuracy is below the ceiling because carelessness cannot be enforced; ceiling is a validity rate, not measured human accuracy, and its sample size is not stated.
Reasoning-type analysis rests on only 500 questions (100 passages).
Baselines are 2016-era single-layer recurrent readers; no seeds, no variance, no batch size or epochs.
Stanford AR underperforms on word-matching questions; authors offer speculative explanations (Sec 5.4).
Datasets scraped from public Chinese websites; copyright of exam items not discussed beyond excluding SSAT, SAT, TOEFL, GRE examples.
Dated: later pretrained models far exceed these baselines; the 43% state of the art reflects 2017 models.

terms.definition: RACE-M denotes the middle school examinations and RACE-H denotes high school examinations
